data.title: Nepal Floods: School children reunited with families after being stranded – Save the Children
data.text:
KATHMANDU, 28 August 2026 –  Nine school children have been reunited with their families after being stranded at school for two days by the devastating flash floods in Northern Nepal, as rescue efforts continue to reach other students, Save the Children said. 
 The children arrived at an aid distribution point where Save the Children is working after walking from their school. Many children in the area travel long distances to their schools and were cut off in the aftermath of the massive surge of floodwater. With support from Save the Children, they were able to find their families. 
 At least 69 schools in flood-devastated districts in Northern Nepal have been destroyed or damaged, putting education at risk for nearly 19,000 children, Save the Children said [1]. 
 The figures are based on an initial assessment and are likely to rise as rescue and response teams reach more areas and more information is available from affected communities [1]. 
 Save the Children staff in Nuwakot said children in the devastated communities are holding onto the few belongings they have or searching for what they lost, including schoolbooks and uniforms. 
 Fears of further flooding are also causing new terror with families moving to higher ground. For many children, this is the first disaster of this scale they have experienced, and they are frightened, distressed and worried about their futures. 
  More than 500 people have died  in Nepal in the disaster, and hundreds are still missing. Some families are camping in tents in front of their damaged homes as efforts continue to find survivors, while others are living with relatives or in community centres. 
  Tara Chettry, Country Director, Save the Children in Nepal said:  
  “Reuniting children with their families in the aftermath of a catastrophe is an urgent and immediate priority, so when disaster strikes, getting children back to school may not seem like the most urgent need. Education is vital. For children who have lost their homes, their belongings and their sense of security, a safe place to learn can be a lifeline.  
  “School gives children something that is desperately important after a disaster: safety, routine, stability. It can help children cope with what they have experienced, while connecting them with the support they need.  
  “Education cannot wait until the emergency is over - it needs to be part of the response from day one.”  
 Save the Children in Nepal’s emergency response team is working in the affected areas and delivering essential items, including household and cooking kits, mosquito nets and blankets to 1,000 households in the first phase of assistance. 
 The humanitarian and child rights organisation is coordinating with national and local authorities to establish the immediate and long-term needs of children and families and is ready to scale up its response. 
 Save the Children has worked in Nepal since 1976. The organisation runs programmes spanning child protection, child rights governance, education, climate change, gender equality, health and nutrition and child poverty. 
  Notes:  
 [1] Figures from the Education Cluster - a joint group of NGOs, UN and the Government of Nepal. The group is co-chaired by Save the Children. The 69 schools have 18,918 students enrolled (9,350 girls and 9,568 boys).

data.title: WVI Nepal Declares Category I National Response to Flash Floods in Rasuwa and Nuwakot
data.text:
A major flash flood entered Nepal through the Bhote Koshi River at around 9:00 AM on 26 August, causing significant damage in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts. The worst-affected areas include Timure, Rasuwagadhi, and Syabrubesi, where homes, markets, roads, and hydropower infrastructure were destroyed. Rescue and relief operations are underway, and authorities have issued alerts for communities along the Trishuli River. 
 World Vision Nepal is closely monitoring the evolving situation and coordinating with government authorities, local partners, and humanitarian actors to assess the needs of affected communities. WV Nepal has declared a Category I National Response and is preparing a 90-day humanitarian response focused on emergency food assistance, shelter support, hygiene and protection services for vulnerable families. 
 According to the latest available reports, at least 177 people have lost their lives in Nepal. More than 800 people remain missing or unaccounted for, including a large number of foreign nationals and dozens of security personnel. Search and rescue operations continue across affected districts as authorities work to verify casualties and locate missing individuals. 
 The disaster has caused extensive damage to lives, livelihoods, and infrastructure exposing children and vulnerable families to increased risks, including displacement, food insecurity, interruption of learning, psychosocial distress, and protection concerns. 
 Prior to the flood, children and households in the affected districts were already facing significant vulnerabilities. In Nuwakot, a 2024 secondary data analysis of 667 children under five years of age from 3,183 households found higher-than-national-average levels of malnutrition, with 32% of children stunted, 12.1% wasted, and 13.9% underweight. These pre-existing nutrition challenges increase the risk of food insecurity and poor health outcomes among children affected by the disaster. 
 Rasuwa also faces significant child protection concerns. National census data indicate that female child marriage remains among the highest in Bagmati Province, placing adolescent girls at heightened risk during emergencies when families experience displacement, loss of livelihoods, and disruption of support systems. The flash flood is therefore expected to exacerbate existing vulnerabilities related to nutrition, child protection, access to education, and essential services, underscoring the need for timely and child-focused humanitarian assistance. 
 While the affected areas are outside World Vision Nepal's current programme locations, the organisation's strong humanitarian response experience and existing partnerships position it well to support relief efforts. The area was previously part of World Vision International Nepal's 2015 earthquake response. 
 During the relief phase, World Vision Nepal plans to support approximately 1,000 affected households with emergency food assistance, shelter kits, hygiene kits, including support for pregnant and lactating women, and dignity kits to address immediate protection and basic needs. 
 Rapid needs assessments are underway to determine the scale of humanitarian needs, particularly among children and other vulnerable households. The recovery phase is expected to include immediate livlihood support and education-focused interventions to help children safely return to learning and restore access to essential services. 
  "The scale and suddenness of this flood have left many families facing immense uncertainty and hardship. As rescue and relief efforts continue, we stand in solidarity with the affected communities and remain committed to supporting efforts that help children and families recover with safety, dignity, and hope,”  says Roslyn H. Gabriel, National Director, WV Nepal.

         Project HOPE's Emergency Response Team is in Nepal, mobilizing a response to devastating landslides and flash floods caused by a massive glacier avalanche.  
  Situational Context  
 On the morning of August 26, 2026, a glacier avalanche near the border between Nepal and China sent tons of rock, mud, and ice into nearby rivers. This disaster triggered massive floods, powerful landslides, and registered a force equal to a 5.2-magnitude earthquake, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. As a result, entire villages have been wiped out and there have been significant impacts to critical infrastructure, including major roads, bridges, and electricity systems. 
 Initial reports put the death toll over 360, with figures expected to rise as search and rescue efforts continue. At least 1,400 people are reported missing, including tourists from as many as 27 different countries, including the United States. Many visitors in the affected area were there for the Nepali festival of Janai Purnima on Friday or on pilgrimage to Tibet’s Mount Kailash, a sacred site for Hindus. 
 Conditions remain dangerous in Nepal, with weather forecasts predicting three days of heavy rain and this disaster making the ongoing monsoon season even  more of a threat to affected communities.  Additionally, yesterday’s landslides formed a new lake, which now poses a significant risk as new bodies of water are at an increased risk of further landslides, mudslides, and flash floods.

 Key Concerns: Impacted communities are in extremely remote, difficult-to-access areas. This has constrained search and rescue efforts. Helicopters are the primary means of access, and adverse weather intermittently grounded flights.

data.title: Students stranded, communities isolated after devastating Nepal floods
data.text:
28 August 2026  - Students cut off from their families and entire communities remain isolated two days after a glacial landslide triggered devastating flash floods that hit parts of northern Nepal and the Chinese border linking Tibet, says Plan International. 
 More than 450 people have been confirmed dead and around 1,000 remain missing, although the full extent of the disaster is still emerging as assessments continue and search operations reach previously inaccessible areas. 
 More than 500 people have been rescued, but many communities remain stranded after roads, bridges and other critical infrastructure were destroyed, severely hampering rescue efforts. 
 Rajendra Paudel, from DEPROSC Nepal, a Plan International partner described the scene he is witnessing in Devighat Bazaar, one of the areas in Nuwakot district that has suffered extensive damage. 
 “There has been extensive human and physical damage across these areas. Just moments ago, a body was recovered from here and taken away. We still do not know how many people are missing. There are many people who have been affected. I have also been in contact with several affected families. They are particularly worried about students who left for school yesterday morning and those who are stranded across the Trishuli River,” he said. 
 Rajendra described the helicopters currently working to recue people and cut off communities but says it has not yet been possible to reach everyone: with all concrete bridges washed away or damaged, there is no way to cross between the two sides of the Trishuli River, leaving many families and children stranded and staying in schools since the flood hit. 
 “The scale of destruction here is enormous…. What we are witnessing here is extremely painful. My relatives were unable to take anything out of their homes and have had to climb up the hillside on the other side to find safety. There is a deep sense of despair among everyone. People are worried about how they will rebuild their lives after this,” he said. 
 There are fears that a lake formed at the site where the floods occurred is rapidly rising and at risk of bursting. 
 “We are very concerned about the possibility of more flooding, along with the stress and trauma this disaster will have on children in particular. Our top priority is ensuring the safety and well-being of children and communities affected by this disaster,” said Plan International Nepal Acting Country Director Srijana Gurung. 
 “We are witnessing in real time the catastrophic impacts of the climate crisis. Climate events are becoming more intense and more frequent, and it is always the most vulnerable people who are disproportionately impacted; the people least responsible for causing climate change,” she added. 
 Plan International Nepal is working to support the Government’s emergency response and send urgently needed supplies to the impacted area’s including distribution of 300 shelter kits, 1,000 hygiene kits and 100 menstrual health management kits for girls and women who have lost their homes. Initial support is planned for around 1,000 affected households whilst the needs are fully assessed. Plan International Nepal is deploying two emergency response team members to support the joint assessment led by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, coordinated through the field hub established by the Catholic Relief Service.

data.title: Statement on the disaster in Nepal and China by Kamal Kishore, Special Representative of the UN Secretary-General for Disaster Risk Reduction and Head of UNDRR
data.text:
I am deeply saddened by the tragic loss of life caused by the devastating flash flood and mudslides that struck parts of Nepal and China. I offer my sincere condolences to the people and Governments of Nepal and China, and to all those affected by this disaster. 
 At this difficult time, I ask the international community to stand in solidarity with the affected countries and communities, supporting their immediate response efforts and longer-term recovery. 
 This disaster is a stark reminder of the transboundary nature of many disaster risks, the fragility of mountain ecosystems, and the challenges of early warning and early action for cascading hazards in mountainous regions. We must continue to work together to address these challenges.

         Situation Overview  
 On the morning of 26 August 2026, a sudden and powerful flash flood swept through the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river systems in central Nepal, affecting settlements across Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading districts, including the Rasuwagadhi border crossing area. Officials suspect that the flooding may have been triggered by an upstream ice or rock avalanche, or by a glacial lake outburst, rather than by local rainfall. The exact cause remains under investigation. 
 At least 165 people have been confirmed dead, while search and rescue operations remain ongoing. A further, 826 people have been reported missing, including 579 tourists. Communication and physical access remain severely constrained, with telephone towers and electricity infrastructure damaged and roads into Rasuwa cut off, delaying assessments and the delivery of humanitarian assistance. 
 Significant damage to critical infrastructure has been reported, including approximately 40 km of road, as well as damage to schools, markets, health facilities, private houses, police posts, weather stations and the Timure customs office. Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) estimates that approximately 10,000 households require immediate relief. The full extent of humanitarian needs and damage remains unclear pending completion of inter-agency assessments.

data.title: Australia’s response to Nepal-China floods (28 August 2026)
data.text:
Joint media release with:  
 The Hon Dr Anne Aly MP, Minister for International Development 
 The Australian Government is rapidly mobilising consular and humanitarian support in response to the catastrophic floods along the Nepal-China border, including through a $5 million assistance package for affected communities. 
 We understand at least 39 Australians are among those reported missing. Australian officials are working urgently to confirm their welfare and provide assistance to those affected. 
 The extraordinary scale of this disaster and the remoteness of the affected region mean immense challenges lie ahead for the response and recovery. 
 The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade is deploying additional personnel to support Australians affected by the disaster. 
 In addition to the staff at the Australian Embassy in Nepal, a Crisis Response Team (CRT) member and a Regional Consular Officer have been deployed and are on the ground in Kathmandu. Further regional and CRT surge support are being prepared for deployment. 
 The Government will send an initial team of three humanitarian response specialists within the next 48 hours to help Australian staff already on the ground. 
 Drawn from the Australia Assists program, the Rapid Response Team has expertise in humanitarian assessment, logistics, communications and planning. 
 As part of the response, the Australian Government will provide $5 million in humanitarian assistance to support urgent disaster response and recovery efforts. 
 The funding will be delivered through established partners to provide support such as food, emergency shelter, clean water and sanitation. 
 These floods have devastated communities along both sides of the border, sweeping away villages, damaging critical infrastructure, and leaving thousands displaced. 
 With roads and bridges destroyed, many communities remain isolated and difficult to reach, underscoring the need for rapid humanitarian assistance. 
 Australia’s assistance includes: 
  $2 million to the World Food Programme, which has already dispatched food rations and provided logistics support for Nepal’s emergency response. 
 $2 million to Australian NGOs through the Australian Humanitarian Partnership to provide support such as emergency shelter, hygiene kits, blankets, medical support and psychosocial support. 
 $1 million to the Emergency Action Alliance to support locally-led recovery and rehabilitation efforts in affected areas.

data.title: En Nepal, las inundaciones repentinas dejan a más de 17.000 niños y niñas necesitados de asistencia humanitaria urgente
data.text:
UNICEF solicita 17,2 millones de dólares para llevar a cabo la respuesta de emergencia y apoyar la recuperación temprana  
  KATMANDÚ, 27 de agosto de 2026 –  Al menos 17.000 niños y niñas se han visto afectados por las devastadoras inundaciones repentinas que arrasaron los distritos nepalíes de Rasuwa, Nuwakot y Dhading el 26 de agosto. Hasta el momento, se calcula que han muerto 332 personas —entre ellas, al menos 14 niños y niñas— y cientos siguen desaparecidas. Se prevé que las cifras aumenten a medida que continúen las operaciones de búsqueda. 
 “En Rasuwa y Dhading, los niños y niñas vieron cómo, en muy poco tiempo, las inundaciones trastocaban por completo sus vidas ante sus propios ojos, causando daños en sus hogares, aulas e instalaciones médicas. Demasiadas personas han perdido la vida y a sus seres queridos”, declaró Alice Akunga, Representante de UNICEF en Nepal. “Mientras la cifra de fallecidos sigue en aumento, sabemos que esta tragedia está lejos de haber terminado. Los niños y niñas que han sobrevivido a las inundaciones se enfrentan ahora a un mayor riesgo de enfermedades, malnutrición, violencia y explotación. UNICEF está sobre el terreno y sigue ampliando su apoyo, pero requerimos con urgencia más recursos para llegar a todos los niños y niñas necesitados”. 
 Las inundaciones repentinas han arrasado comunidades enteras o las han dejado aisladas, y han causado graves daños en carreteras, puentes, instalaciones hidroeléctricas, sistemas de abastecimiento de agua y redes de telecomunicaciones, por lo que las zonas afectadas son ahora prácticamente inaccesibles y la entrega de ayuda vital se ha visto dificultada. Al menos cuatro centros de salud han sufrido graves daños, lo que impide que los niños, niñas y sus familias tengan acceso a la atención médica cuando más la necesitan. 
 Además, 18 escuelas han quedado completamente destruidas y otras 20 han sufrido daños, privando a los niños y niñas de espacios seguros donde aprender, jugar y recuperarse. A esto se suma que decenas de escuelas están situadas cerca de las riberas de los ríos en las zonas afectadas y siguen en riesgo. Según las estimaciones, 10.000 niños y niñas en edad escolar necesitan ahora apoyo urgente para continuar su educación, en particular acceso a centros temporales de aprendizaje, reposición de materiales educativos y apoyo psicosocial tanto para el alumnado como para el personal docente. 
 En estrecha colaboración con el Gobierno de Nepal y los aliados humanitarios, UNICEF está ampliando la ayuda vital en los ámbitos de la salud, la nutrición, el agua, el saneamiento y la higiene (WASH), la educación, la protección de la infancia y la protección social. En los próximos días, se enviarán a las comunidades más afectadas suministros previamente almacenados, como tiendas de campaña para prestar atención médica, mosquiteros, kits para recién nacidos y alimentos terapéuticos para niños y niñas con malnutrición aguda. Los kits de higiene de emergencia destinados a miles de hogares que los necesitan ya se están distribuyendo. 
 Mientras tanto, se han movilizado equipos de salud mental y apoyo psicosocial, y UNICEF trabaja para identificar y registrar a los niños y niñas desaparecidos o separados de sus familias, y reunirlos con ellas. UNICEF también está colaborando con el Gobierno de Nepal para proporcionar asistencia en efectivo de emergencia a los hogares afectados, con el fin de ayudar a las familias a satisfacer sus necesidades básicas urgentes y evitar que recurran a estrategias de supervivencia perjudiciales. 
 En este contexto, UNICEF solicita 17,2 millones de dólares para mantener su respuesta de emergencia y apoyar la recuperación temprana hasta que se evalúe el alcance total de las necesidades. Sin financiación urgente y flexible, UNICEF verá gravemente limitada su capacidad para prestar servicios esenciales de salud, nutrición, WASH, educación, protección de la infancia y protección social a los niños y niñas —incluidos los niños y niñas con discapacidad— y a las mujeres.

data.title: Au Népal, 17 000 enfants ont besoin d’une aide humanitaire d’urgence en raison des crues éclair qui ont frappé le pays
data.text:
L’UNICEF lance un appel de fonds de 17,2 millions de dollars des États-Unis pour déployer une intervention d’urgence et soutenir les premiers efforts de relèvement.  
  KATHMANDOU, le 27 août 2026 –  Au moins 17 000 enfants ont été touchés par les crues éclair dévastatrices qui ont ravagé les districts népalais de Rasuwa, Nuwakot et Dhading le 26 août. À ce jour, on estime à 332 le nombre de décès – dont au moins 14 enfants – tandis que des centaines de personnes sont toujours portées disparues. Ce bilan devrait augmenter à mesure que les opérations de recherche se poursuivent. 
 « À Rasuwa et à Dhading, les enfants ont vu leur vie littéralement disparaître sous leurs yeux en un instant, alors que leurs maisons, leurs salles de classe et leurs infrastructures médicales ont été emportées par les eaux. Un grand nombre d’entre eux ont perdu la vie, ou ont perdu des êtres chers », a déclaré Alice Akunga, Représentante de l’UNICEF au Népal. « Alors que le bilan ne cesse de s’alourdir, nous savons que cette tragédie est loin d’être terminée. Les enfants qui ont survécu aux inondations sont désormais confrontés à des risques accrus de maladies, de malnutrition, de violence et d’exploitation. Si l’UNICEF est d’ores et déjà sur le terrain et œuvre à renforcer son soutien, des ressources supplémentaires sont nécessaires de toute urgence pour atteindre chaque enfant dans le besoin. » 
 Les crues éclair ont dévasté des communautés entières et coupé de nombreuses autres du reste du pays. Les routes, les ponts, les installations hydroélectriques, les systèmes d’approvisionnement en eau et les réseaux de télécommunications ayant été gravement endommagés, les zones touchées sont en grande partie inaccessibles, une situation entrave l’acheminement de l’aide vitale. Par ailleurs, au moins quatre établissements de santé ont été sévèrement touchés, ce qui complique l’accès aux soins des enfants et des familles au moment où ils en ont le plus besoin. 
 De plus, 18 écoles ont été entièrement détruites et 20 autres ont subi d’importants dégâts, privant les enfants d’espaces sûrs pour apprendre, jouer et se rétablir. Des dizaines d’autres établissements situés à proximité des berges dans les zones touchées demeurent en outre menacés. Aussi, selon les estimations, 10 000 enfants d’âge scolaire ont aujourd’hui besoin d’une aide d’urgence pour poursuivre leur scolarité, notamment d’un accès à des centres d’apprentissage temporaires, de matériel pédagogique de remplacement, ainsi que de services de soutien psychosocial à l’intention des élèves et des enseignants. 
 L’UNICEF travaille en étroite collaboration avec le Gouvernement népalais et ses partenaires humanitaires afin de renforcer son aide vitale sur le terrain dans les domaines de la santé, de la nutrition, de l’eau, de l’assainissement et de l’hygiène (EAH), de l'éducation, de la protection de l’enfance et de la protection sociale. Dans les prochains jours, des fournitures prépositionnées seront acheminées vers les communautés les plus durement touchées, notamment des tentes médicales, des moustiquaires, des kits pour nouveau-nés et des aliments thérapeutiques destinés aux enfants souffrant de malnutrition aiguë. Des trousses d’hygiène d’urgence destinées à des milliers de foyers dans le besoin sont d’ores et déjà en cours de distribution. 
 Parallèlement, des équipes spécialisées dans la santé mentale et le soutien psychosocial ont été mobilisées, tandis que l’UNICEF s’efforce d’identifier, d’enregistrer et de réunir les enfants disparus ou séparés de leur famille. L’UNICEF collabore également avec le Gouvernement népalais pour faire parvenir des transferts monétaires d’urgence aux foyers touchés, et ainsi aider les familles à subvenir à leurs besoins fondamentaux sans qu’elles n’aient besoin de recourir à des stratégies d’adaptation néfastes. 
 Dans ce contexte, et en attendant que l’ampleur exacte des besoins ait été évaluée, l’UNICEF lance un appel de fonds de 17,2 millions de dollars É.-U. afin de poursuivre son intervention d’urgence et de soutenir les premiers efforts de relèvement. Sans financements souples et immédiats, la capacité de l’UNICEF à fournir aux enfants, y compris à ceux en situation de handicap et aux femmes, des services essentiels dans les domaines de la santé, de la nutrition, de l’EAH, de l’éducation, de la protection de l’enfance et de la protection sociale, sera fortement limitée.

data.title: IFRC launches CHF 25 million Emergency Appeal in response to devastating Nepal flash floods
data.text:
Katmandu/Kuala Lumpur/Geneva, 27 August 2026  – The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) has launched an  Emergency Appeal for CHF 25 million  to support the Nepal Red Cross Society’s response to the devastating flash floods that struck northern Nepal, just  a day after releasing nearly CHF 1 million in emergency funding  to support the immediate lifesaving response. 
 Current estimates suggest around 93,000 people may have been affected, while assessments continue in hard-to-reach areas. Many homes have been destroyed or severely damaged, and multiple bridges have been washed away and major roads damaged, cutting off some of the worst-affected communities. The remoteness of the affected areas, combined with damaged infrastructure, is making it harder both to assess the full scale of the disaster and to deliver assistance to people who need it most. 
  “The IFRC Emergency appeal is a critical step to support the communities affected, focusing not only on the emergency response, but also on the mid and long-term recovery. While we are getting a clearer picture of the scale of devastation, we know that entire villages were washed away and needs will grow in the coming hours and days. Communities that have lost homes and livelihoods will need sustained support as they recover and rebuild. We call on the international community to show solidarity in the months to come” , said Jagan Chapagain, IFRC Secretary General. 
 The 24-month IFRC Emergency Appeal will support the Nepal Red Cross response across shelter, cash assistance, health, household relief items, water, sanitation and hygiene, mental health and psychosocial support, and restoring family links. The appeal has a strong focus not only on meeting immediate humanitarian needs, but also on supporting medium- and longer-term recovery. 
 IFRC has immediately mobilized its entire global network to support Nepal Red Cross and will adapt the response as further information becomes available. 
 Nepal Red Cross teams have been responding since the immediate aftermath of the disaster, providing food and water and distributing emergency supplies including tarpaulins, blankets, first aid kits, stretchers, emergency WASH kits and body bags. Communication with teams in affected areas has been difficult due to limited phone signals, and additional teams are being mobilised to support those already on the ground.

  1. Executive Summary  
 On 26 August 2026, an ice-and-rock landslide in the upper transboundary watershed near the Nepal–China border triggered a major debris-laden flash flood through the Bhote Koshi–Trishuli–Narayani river system. As of 27 August, at 09:00 Nepal time, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA), provisional figures report 10,000 households require immediate relief, 165 bodies recovered, 247 people out of contact, 73 injured, and extensive infrastructure damage, including 35 motorable bridges and 45 suspension bridges swept away and approximately 40 km of paved road damaged. Evacuation orders and downstream alerts remain active because the upstream blockage lake may not have fully drained. QC has approved a USD 69,000 quick life-saving intervention for immediate food and emergency shelter assistance. An additional USD 1,000,000 is urgently needed to expand the relief response and support priority early recovery interventions, bringing the total planned intervention to USD 1,069,000.

         UNICEF appeals for US$17.2 million to deliver emergency response and early recovery  
  KATHMANDU, 27 August 2026 –  At least 17,000 children have been impacted by the devastating flash floods that tore through Nepal's Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading districts on 26 August. So far, an estimated 332 people have died – including at least 14 children - and-hundreds are still missing. The numbers are expected to rise as search operations continue. 
 “Children across Rasuwa and Dhading saw their lives being literally washed away in front of their eyes in a very short span of time, with homes, classrooms, and medical facilities damaged. Too many lost their lives and loved ones,” said Alice Akunga, UNICEF Representative to Nepal. “With the death toll still rising, we know this tragedy is far from over. Children who have survived the floods now face heightened risks of disease, malnutrition, violence and exploitation. UNICEF is on the ground and scaling up support, but we urgently need more resources to reach every child in need.” 
 The flash floods have swept away or cut off entire communities, with roads, bridges, hydropower facilities, water systems and telecommunications networks badly damaged, leaving affected areas largely inaccessible and hampering the delivery of life-saving aid. At least four health facilities have been severely damaged, preventing children and families from accessing healthcare when they need it most. 
 In addition, 18 schools have been completely destroyed and a further 20 have sustained damage, depriving children of safe spaces to learn, play and recover. Dozens of schools are located close to riverbanks in the affected areas and remain at risk. An estimated 10,000 school-age children now require urgent support to continue their education, including access to temporary learning centres, replacement learning materials, and psychosocial support for both children and teachers. 
 Working closely with the Government of Nepal and humanitarian partners, UNICEF is scaling up life-saving support across health, nutrition, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), education, child protection and social protection. In the coming days, pre-positioned supplies will be dispatched to the hardest-hit communities, including medical tents, bed nets and newborn kits, and therapeutic food for children with acute malnutrition. Emergency hygiene kits for thousands of households are already reaching those in need. 
 Meanwhile, mental health and psychosocial support teams have been mobilized, and UNICEF is working to identify, register and reunite children missing or separated from their families. UNICEF is also working with the Government of Nepal to deliver emergency cash assistance to affected households to help families meet urgent basic needs and avoid resorting to harmful coping strategies. 
 UNICEF is appealing for US$17.2 million to sustain its emergency response and support early recovery until the full extent of needs are assessed. Without urgent and flexible funding, UNICEF's ability to deliver essential health, nutrition, WASH, education, child protection and social protection services to children — including children with disabilities — and women will be severely constrained.

data.title: Oxfam Intermón responde a la riada de Nepal en Rasuwa y Nuwakot, donde las carreteras y los puentes destruidos dificultan las labores de socorro.
data.text:
Oxfam Intermón ha puesto en marcha una respuesta de emergencia en Rasuwa y Nuwakot, los distritos más afectados por la riada del miércoles, donde carreteras y puentes arrasados ​​por la crecida han dejado  comunidades enteras prácticamente inaccesibles.  
 Al menos 200 personas han muerto y cientos más están desaparecidas en Nepal y el Tíbet. La crecida arrasó el río Trishuli a través de Timure, Syaprubesi y Bhairabkunda, poniendo en peligro a las familias que viven a lo largo de las riberas de Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha y Chitwan. 
 «Barrios enteros están sepultados bajo el lodo y los equipos de rescate siguen trabajando. El agua subió nueve metros en media hora. Lo que vemos hasta ahora es solo lo que podemos alcanzar», dice  Santosh Pandey, responsable humanitario de Oxfam en Nepal.  
 El colapso de carreteras, puentes y comunicaciones ha dificultado gravemente las labores de socorro. El Gobierno de Nepal ha solicitado 30 puentes provisionales de entre 50 y 70 metros cada uno, además de alimentos, refugio y suministros para la purificación del agua. Por ahora,  el acceso a las comunidades más afectadas depende casi por completo del transporte aéreo.  
 “Los ríos están llenos de escombros y aguas residuales, y no queda suministro de agua potable por tuberías. La prioridad ahora es proporcionar agua potable y saneamiento seguro a la mayoría de las personas afectadas en estos valles”, añade Pandey. 
 Las familias también necesitan artículos de higiene, refugio de emergencia y alimentos.  El Gobierno de Nepal estima que 8.692 hogares —casi 40.000 personas— requieren apoyo de emergencia  en materia de higiene y purificación del agua, además de 3.130 kits de higiene personal y casi 4.000 kits para bebés menores de cinco años. 
 Oxfam, en colaboración con sus socios y en estrecha coordinación con las autoridades locales, está suministrando de inmediato kits de higiene de emergencia, que incluyen soluciones de purificación de agua, a 200 hogares en el distrito de Rasuwa, el más afectado. Sin embargo, la organización necesita urgentemente más de un millón de euros para ampliar su respuesta y llegar a 10.000 personas con refugio temporal, agua potable y kits de higiene y saneamiento.

 Tenemos portavoces disponibles para entrevistas. 
 Oxfam Intermón ha abierto una campaña de recogida de fondos para atender a las personas afectadas por esta emergencia. Enlace:  https://www.oxfamintermon.org/es/emergencia/riada-nepal  
 Oxfam trabaja en Nepal desde la década de 1980, junto con las comunidades y socios locales, para abordar la desigualdad y desarrollar programas humanitarios y de desarrollo. Su labor se basa en el fortalecimiento del espacio cívico y el apoyo a las personas para que desafíen las injusticias que las mantienen en la pobreza, con un enfoque feminista arraigado en el Sur Global. Oxfam en Nepal trabaja en tres áreas interrelacionadas: clima y agua, justicia de género y respuesta humanitaria y gestión del riesgo de desastres.

data.title: Islamic Relief sending emergency aid to Nepal flood survivors
data.text:
Islamic Relief is sending emergency aid to communities affected by the deadly flash floods in Nepal that swept away people and homes within seconds. 
 At least 359 people are confirmed killed so far, but many more are still missing and the death toll is still rising. At least 50,000 people are badly affected, with many families losing their homes and livelihoods. There are now fears another lake is at risk of bursting, which would cause further destruction and loss of life. 
 Eye witnesses describe a 30-metre (100 foot) high wall of water instantly washing away people, homes and markets and destroying critical infrastructure. The surge of floodwater was so powerful it damaged villages high in the mountains, far above the usual river level. Roads, bridges and power networks have been badly damaged or blocked by rubble, making it hard to reach survivors in remote areas. 
 Islamic Relief’s immediate response will provide emergency shelter and aid such as blankets and mattresses to people in the worst-hit districts of Rasuwa and Nuwakot, working in full coordination with Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) and District Disaster Management Committee (DDMC). 
  Golam Motasim Billah, Islamic Relief’s country director in Nepal, says:  
  “Torrents of water swept through villages without any warning and families lost everything within just a few seconds. The floods were so powerful they even tore through a major bridge and damaged villages high up in the mountains.  
  “Survivors are desperately trying to trace their missing loved ones, while at the same time trying to find a safe place for their families to shelter and get food for their children. Power supplies have been badly damaged, plunging areas into darkness.  
  “Our prayers are with everyone affected and we are working with authorities on the ground to get aid to people as quickly as possible.  
  “People urgently need aid such as shelter, ready-to-eat food, safe drinking water, and hygiene kits to stop diseases spreading. As well as the immediate loss of life, people’s livelihoods have been washed away. Communities will need long term support to recover.”  
 The cause of the disaster has not yet been confirmed, but Nepal is increasingly vulnerable to the impacts of climate change, with melting glaciers causing flooding and landslides. Scientists in the region have reported that a huge chunk of glacier fell up to 7,000 feet into the river below, causing a massive wave of water to surge downstream. 
 As more information emerges, Islamic Relief stands ready to scale up assistance further as needed. 
  Islamic Relief has worked in Nepal since 2015 when it responded to the Gorkha earthquake. Last year the charity worked with local partner organisations to support over 113,000 people in Nepal, through projects providing education, safe water and helping communities adapt to climate change and more frequent disasters.

data.title: Népal : l’IFRC débloque des fonds d’urgence alors que les inondations soudaines laissent des communautés isolées
data.text:
Katmandou/Genève, 26 août 2026  – La Fédération internationale des Sociétés de la Croix-Rouge et du Croissant-Rouge (IFRC) débloque près d’un million de francs suisses de financement d’urgence afin de soutenir la réponse de la  Croix-Rouge népalaise (CRN)  aux graves inondations soudaines qui ont frappé le nord du Népal. 
 Ce financement, alloué grâce au  Fonds d’urgence pour les réponses aux catastrophes de l’IFRC-DREF , permettra à la Croix-Rouge népalaise de répondre aux besoins urgents, tandis que les équipes évaluent l’ampleur des dégâts et identifient les communautés nécessitant une assistance. 
 La rupture d’un lac glaciaire, dont les eaux provenaient de la zone du Xizang/Tibet à la frontière chinoise, a provoqué d’importantes destructions dans le nord du Népal le 26 août. Les districts de Rasuwa et de Nuwakot figurent parmi les zones les plus durement touchées. Des habitations, des routes, des ponts, des installations hydroélectriques et d’autres infrastructures essentielles ont été gravement endommagés. 
 Plusieurs ponts ont été emportés et des axes routiers majeurs ont été coupés, rendant certaines des communautés les plus durement touchées extrêmement difficiles d’accès, en particulier dans le district de Rasuwa. Ces contraintes d’accès compliquent l’évaluation de l’ampleur réelle de la catastrophe et l’acheminement de l’aide aux personnes qui en ont besoin. 
  « La priorité est désormais d’atteindre les communautés touchées et de fournir une assistance aux personnes qui ont perdu leur logement, ont été blessées ou se retrouvent isolées » , a déclaré David Fisher, chef de la délégation de l’IFRC au Népal. 
  « Le déblocage de ces fonds d’urgence permet à la Croix-Rouge népalaise d’agir immédiatement pendant que les évaluations se poursuivent. Nous suivons la situation de près et sommes prêts à apporter un soutien supplémentaire si les besoins augmentent. Nous n’oublierons pas non plus de soutenir leur relèvement à long terme, car des villages entiers et des zones commerciales ont été entièrement détruits. »  
 Les équipes de la Croix-Rouge népalaise ont été déployées vers les zones touchées, tandis que des équipes d’urgence et des volontaires supplémentaires sont mobilisés afin de soutenir les branches locales dont les capacités de réponse sont limitées. 
 L’assistance initiale comprend la distribution d’eau potable et de fournitures d’urgence, notamment des bâches, des couvertures, des nattes de couchage, des trousses de premiers secours, des brancards et des sacs mortuaires. 
 Les priorités humanitaires immédiates sont la fourniture d’abris d’urgence, l’accès à l’eau potable, la distribution d’articles de première nécessité, les premiers secours et l’assistance sanitaire, ainsi que le rétablissement de l’accès aux communautés isolées. Des évaluations rapides sont en cours de préparation afin de déterminer l’ampleur des besoins et d’orienter la prochaine phase de la réponse, notamment une éventuelle assistance en espèces. 
 L’IFRC soutient la Croix-Rouge népalaise à travers un financement d’urgence, une coordination opérationnelle et un appui technique. Parallèlement, les équipes régionales et mondiales restent prêtes à fournir des capacités supplémentaires et une assistance internationale si nécessaire. 
 Une vision plus précise de l’impact de la catastrophe devrait se dégager à mesure que les eaux se retireront et que les zones actuellement inaccessibles pourront être atteintes. La situation reste très évolutive, et l’IFRC continue de suivre de près son évolution et d’adapter la réponse à mesure que de nouvelles informations deviennent disponibles.

data.title: Oxfam launches Nepal flood response in worst-hit Rasuwa and Nuwakot, as destroyed roads and swept-away bridges block relief efforts
data.text:
Oxfam is launching an emergency response in Rasuwa and Nuwakot, the districts worst affected by Wednesday's flash flood, as roads and bridges swept away by the surge have left entire communities almost impossible to reach. 
 On Wednesday 26 August, a landslide and glacial event around 20km north of the Rasuwagadhi checkpoint blocked the Lhende Khola, triggering a major flash flood. At least 200 people have been killed and hundreds more are missing across Nepal and Tibet. The surge then swept into the Trishuli River via Timure, Syaprubesi and Bhairabkunda, leaving families along the riverbanks of Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha and Chitwan, in peril. 
 “Entire neighbourhoods are under mud and rescue teams are still digging. The water rose nine metres in half an hour. What we are seeing so far is only what we can reach,” said Santosh Pandey, Oxfam Humanitarian Lead in Nepal. 
 The collapse of roads, bridges and communications has severely hampered relief efforts. The Government of Nepal's has asked for 30 temporary bridges of 50 to 70 metres each, alongside food, shelter and water purification supplies. For now, reaching the hardest-hit communities depends almost entirely on-air access. 
 “The rivers are full of debris and sewage, and there is no piped supply left to fall back on. Getting clean water and safe sanitation to most affected people into these valleys is the priority now,” added Pandey. 
 Families also need hygiene supplies, emergency shelter and food. The Government of Nepal estimates that 8,692 households – nearly 40,000 people – require emergency hygiene support and water purification, in addition to 3,130 dignity kits and nearly 4,000 baby kits for children under five. 
 Oxfam, working with its partners and in close coordination with local authorities, is immediately supplying emergency hygiene kits, incorporating water purification solutions, for 200 households in the hardest-hit Rasuwa district. But Oxfam urgently needs £1 million British pounds to scale up its response and reach 10,000 people with temporary shelter, clean water, and sanitation and hygiene kits. 
  Notes to editors  
  Oxfam has worked in Nepal since the 1980s, alongside communities and local partners to tackle inequality and deliver humanitarian and development programmes. Its work is grounded in strengthening civic space and supporting people to challenge the injustices that keep them in poverty, led by a feminist approach rooted in the Global South. Oxfam in Nepal works across three connected areas: climate and water, gender justice, and humanitarian response and disaster risk management. 
 Oxfam is working closely with the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA), the Social Welfare Council and District Administration Offices to deliver relief materials to affected communities.

data.title: Nepal floods: Rescuers race to find survivors with areas still cut off
data.text:
Rescuers are racing to find survivors in the flash flood-devastated areas of Northern Nepal, as Save the Children delivers emergency aid to families, with many places still only accessible by helicopter. 
  KATHMANDU, 27 August 2026 –  Rescuers are racing to find survivors in the flash flood-devastated areas of Northern Nepal, as Save the Children delivers emergency aid to families, with many places still only accessible by helicopter. 
 The disaster in the Rasuwa region struck at a time when children were either on their way to school or starting lessons. Many children in the area travel long distances to school - areas that are now cut off by flood waters, potentially separating them from their families or caregivers. Damage to phone and internet infrastructure is also making it challenging for families to contact relatives. 
 Families are finding shelter wherever they can. Some have moved in with relatives; others are living in public buildings such as community centres. Access to clean water has been severely disrupted across the district. Save the Children staff working in the flood affected areas say there are significant challenges in reaching communities in need of aid. Roads have been blocked or flooded, and severe traffic congestion is slowing rescue and relief efforts as some people flee affected areas and others travel towards them to support rescue operations. 
 As the  number of people confirmed dead rises , hundreds of people are still reported missing. The massive flash floods came without warning, sweeping through communities in the mountainous region and leaving behind destroyed homes and buildings, broken bridges and a sea of mud and debris. 
 Tara Chettry, Country Director, Save the Children in Nepal, said: 
 “Children’s lives changed in an instant. Some have lost their homes and belongings and a sense of security. For a child, losing a home is not just losing a building, it is losing the place where they feel safe. 
 “In the aftermath of a disaster like this, children are among the most vulnerable and face heightened risks to their health, safety, protection, and wellbeing. They will be confused and distressed after witnessing such devastation. Identifying any separated or unaccompanied children must be a priority for the rescue and response teams. 
 “While immediate assistance is urgently needed, the response cannot stop with emergency supplies. There will be no quick recovery for many of these communities and children and families will need sustained support well beyond the first days and weeks of this crisis, to meet their urgent needs, rebuild their lives, return to school and recover from this devastating disaster. 
 “Flexible funding is critical. It will allow us and our local partners to respond to longer term needs as the situation evolves, while investing in recovery and resilience so communities can rebuild safer and stronger.” 
 Save the Children in Nepal’s emergency response team is working in the affected areas and delivering essential items, including household and cooking kits, mosquito nets and blankets to 1,000 households in the first phase of assistance. 
 The humanitarian and child rights organisation is coordinating with national and local authorities to establish the immediate and long-term needs of children and families and is ready to scale up its response.

data.title: MSF team in Nepal
data.text:
27 August 2026 - After a major flashflood struck the Rasuwa district in Nepal, an MSF team experienced in providing emergency responses has arrived in Nepal to assess people’s immediate needs. MSF stands ready to provide urgent humanitarian and medical assistance. ​ 
 The floods rapidly impacted Timure, Rasuwagadhi and Syabrubesi areas causing significant damage to settlements, markets and infrastructure. Flood waves are estimated to have been as large as 8-10 metres in some locations. Hundreds of people are feared to have died with many people still missing. ​ 
 Floodwaters reached the town of Mugling in Chitwan district and have since begun to recede, though authorities say the risk remains high, as the blocked section of the river upstream has not yet been fully cleared. ​ 
 High-alert warnings have been issued for communities located along the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers, particularly in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha and Chitwan districts. People living along riverbanks have been advised to move to safer locations. 
 Authorities are carrying out urgent search and rescue operations in affected areas and a full health emergency response has been initiated. ​ 
 The MSF team arrived in Nepal less than 24 hours after the floods struck, and we are engaging with health facilities to assess if we can support. We know from our years of experience in emergencies that people in affected areas will have urgent needs for shelter, non food items, access to clean water and latrines, and emergency medical and trauma support. ​ 
 MSF teams are assessing how we can provide assistance to people and stand ready to support the national response to this tragedy. ​ 
 ENDS

        SITUATION OVERVIEW

 • According to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA), 10,000 households require immediate relief. At least 157 deaths have been confirmed and nearly 245 people remain missing, including security personnel, customs officials, foreign tourists and residents, while search and rescue operations continue (RisingNepal).

data.title: Nepal Flash Floods: Rapid Situation Overview (27 August 2026)
data.text:
Attachments 
   
         
       
                          
           
                   
               
                   

   

         Download Report 
         (PDF | 671.01 KB) 
       
     
       
 


      
        A series of flash floods struck the Bhote Koshi River in Rasuwa district, northern Nepal, on the morning of 26 August 2026, entering from the Tibet Autonomous Region of China at around 09:00 Nepal Standard Time (NPT) and surging downstream through the Trishuli River system into Nuwakot, Dhading and beyond. The border settlements of Timure and Syabrubesi, the Rasuwagadhi customs and border crossing, and roughly a dozen riverside settlements in northern Rasuwa took the earliest and heaviest impact, before the surge moved through Betrawati and Trishuli Bazar in Nuwakot, Galchhi and Dhunge Bazaar in Dhading, and onward past Muglin into the Narayani river system, where deaths were subsequently recorded as far away as Chitwan, Gorkha, Tanahu and Nawalparasi East. 
 Casualty figures rose sharply and repeatedly through the day as search teams reached previously cut-off areas, and this report treats every figure below as provisional. By the morning of Thursday 27 August, the NDRRMA and Nepal Police put the confirmed death toll at 165, with 73 people injured, up from the roughly 160 (157 bodies recovered) reported late on Wednesday, and superseding Wednesday-evening figures of 95 from the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) and 72 from the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA). Hundreds of people remain unaccounted for. As of a Nepal Police bulletin issued around 08:15 on Thursday 27 August, 826 people were listed as missing in Nepal alone: 579 travellers (466 foreign nationals and 113 Nepalis), 85 security personnel (44 Nepali Army, 28 Nepal Police and 13 Armed Police Force), 161 residents of Rasuwa and one of Nuwakot. Most of the missing foreign travellers were moving toward the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage route through Tibet, and included at least 133 Indian pilgrims alongside citizens of Malaysia (55), the United States (47), Australia (34), the United Kingdom (33), Canada (24) and other countries. A further 85 security personnel (Nepali Army, Nepal Police and Armed Police Force), 60 hydropower-project workers, 26 bank employees and 15 customs officers were separately reported missing or out of contact A further 60 hydropower-project workers, 26 bank employees and 15 customs officers were separately reported out of contact. On the Chinese side of the border, state media (CCTV) reported 3 confirmed deaths and 558 people missing, 260 of them foreign nationals, around the Gyirong Port trade hub in Xizang (Tibet), bringing the combined Nepal-and-Tibet missing total to more than 1,300, though the two countries’ counts of foreign nationals may overlap. 
 The flood caused severe damage to infrastructure across a roughly 60-kilometer valley corridor. The Department of Roads confirmed that the entire 42-kilometer road linking Betrawati (Nuwakot) to the Rasuwagadhi border crossing had been destroyed at multiple points, including several concrete bridges, cutting Nepal’s principal overland trade and pilgrimage route to Tibet; a further 16-kilometer stretch toward the border, recently upgraded with Chinese government financing, was also swept away. The Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) reported damage to 14 hydropower projects with a combined capacity of approximately 748 MW (9 operational plants (354 MW) and 5 under construction (394 MW)) including the Rasuwagadhi, Chilime, Sanjen Khola, Upper Trishuli-1, Trishuli and Devighat plants and a 220 kV substation; the Ministry of Energy’s earlier same-day estimate had put the loss at 431 MW, illustrating how fast the damage assessment was still moving. Nine commercial bank branches were swept away, with 26 staff unaccounted for, and the Rasuwa customs office in Timure lost contact with 15 employees. 
 The trigger has not been officially confirmed. Nepal’s Department of Hydrology and Meteorology and independent glaciologists advanced a preliminary hypothesis, based on satellite imagery shared by Chinese counterparts through the International Center for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), that an ice-and-rock avalanche blocked the Lhende Khola, a Bhote Koshi tributary on the Nepal-China border, roughly 20 km upstream of the Miteri Bridge, forming a temporary debris-dammed lake that subsequently burst The US Geological Survey initially logged a magnitude-4.4 earthquake at 08:37 local time shortly before the flood, but has since revised its analysis, concluding that the seismic signal was in fact a magnitude-5.2 glacial collapse, not a tectonic earthquake, based on nearby seismic stations, long-period seismic waves and satellite imagery. Meteorologists ruled out heavy local rainfall as the cause in Rasuwa itself, while noting that satellite data showed rainfall on the Tibetan side of the border. A broadly similar flood on the same river in July 2025 was ultimately attributed to the drainage of a supraglacial lake; ICIMOD scientists say such cascading glacial hazards are increasing at an “unprecedented” pace across the Hindu Kush Himalaya region. 
 The Government of Nepal has mobilized the Nepali Army, Armed Police Force and Nepal Police, supported by military and private helicopters, for search, rescue and relief operations, and the Cabinet has ordered free medical treatment for the injured, financial assistance to bereaved families, and the reopening of roads, restoration of power and telecommunications, and provision of food and shelter for those displaced. Nepal has asked China and India for assistance; China has pledged relief funding, and India is sending humanitarian supplies, while Indian authorities in neighboring Bihar state have opened the Valmikinagar Barrage on the Gandak River as a precaution and prepared to evacuate up to 10,000–12,000 people downstream. The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) has released emergency funding to the Nepal Red Cross Society, which has begun distributing water, tarpaulins, blankets and first-aid supplies, though many of the worst-affected communities in Rasuwa remain difficult to reach because roads and bridges are destroyed. As of the data cut-off, no government or humanitarian body had published a consolidated total for people displaced, sheltering or in need, and this report treats that figure as a priority information gap for the days ahead.

data.title: Floods and massive landslide devastate communities along Nepal-China border
data.text:
A major flash flood and glacial landslide has struck parts of northern Nepal and the Chinese border linking Tibet, with hundreds of people reported missing and early reports indicating multiple fatalities. As search and rescue efforts begin Plan International stands in solidarity with all those affected by this disaster. 
 Plan International Nepal Acting Country Director, Srijana Gurung said: 
 “This is a deeply tragic disaster affecting communities across Timure, Rasuwagadhi and Syabrubesi in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading. We all remember the catastrophic earthquake 11 years ago that killed almost 10,000 people. Many of the communities impacted by yesterday’s disaster were also severely affected by the 2015 earthquake. No person deserves to go through an event like this, let alone two. 
 Across Nepal, communities are facing climate shock after shock with barely any time to recover. Floods and landslides have always happened in Nepal but the climate crisis is making them far more frequent and intense. 
 So far, we know the flash flood from the Bhote Koshi River has caused extensive damage to villages, markets, roads, communications infrastructure and hydropower facilities in Nepal. However, it is still too early to know the full scale of the destruction, but we fear the impact may be severe, with many people killed and injured. 
 Rescue and relief efforts 
 As communities grapple with the devastating impact of this disaster, the Government of Nepal has moved swiftly to support rescue and relief efforts, deploying security forces and issuing warnings to communities downstream along the Trishuli River. The priority now must be reaching those affected, supporting families searching for loved ones, and ensuring vulnerable communities have the assistance they need. 
 Plan International stands in solidarity with all those affected by this devastating disaster. Our thoughts are with the children, young people, families, tourists and communities facing loss, uncertainty and disruption. Families today will have lost loved ones but also their homes, and livelihoods and will be in urgent need of medical attention, shelter, water, food and hygiene kits. There is also a risk of waterborne disease as access to clean water and sanitation is likely to have been damaged. 
 We are in close communication with the Government of Nepal and are closely monitoring the situation to support a coordinated, needs-based response. 
 At this difficult time, we recognise the strength and resilience of communities across Nepal and remain committed to working alongside government authorities, partners and local communities to ensure children and their families are protected and supported. Particular attention must be given to those most at risk, including girls, women, older people and people with disabilities, while ensuring their rights, safety, dignity and voices remain at the centre of the response.”

data.title: Nepal: IFRC releases emergency funds as flash floods leave communities isolated
data.text:
Katmandu/Geneva, 26 August 2026  – The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) is releasing nearly CHF one million in emergency funding to support the  Nepal Red Cross Society ’s response to severe flash flooding in northern Nepal. 
 The funding, provided through the IFRC’s  Disaster Response Emergency Fund (DREF) , will help the Nepal Red Cross respond to urgent needs while teams assess the scale of the destruction and identify communities requiring assistance. 
 A glacial lake outburst flood originating from the Chinese border from the Xizang/Tibet area caused significant destruction in northern Nepal on 26 August, with some of the worst impacts reported in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts. Homes, roads, bridges, hydropower facilities and other critical infrastructure have been badly damaged. 
 Multiple bridges have been washed away and major roads disrupted, leaving some of the worst-affected communities extremely difficult to reach, especially in Rasuwa. These access constraints are making it harder for responders to assess the full scale of the disaster and deliver assistance to people in need. 
  “The priority now is to reach affected communities and get assistance to people who have lost their homes, suffered injuries or have been cut off,”  said the IFRC head of delegation for Nepal, David Fisher. 
  “The release of emergency funding means the Nepal Red Cross can act immediately while assessments continue. We are closely monitoring the situation and are ready to provide additional support if needs increase. We will not forget support for their long-term recovery either, since entire villages and market areas have been wiped out”.  
 Nepal Red Cross teams have deployed towards affected areas, while additional emergency teams and volunteers are being mobilised to support local branches with limited response capacity. 
 Initial assistance includes distributing drinking water and emergency supplies including tarpaulins, blankets, sleeping mats, first aid kits, stretchers and body bags. 
 The immediate humanitarian priorities are emergency shelter, safe drinking water, basic relief items, first aid and health support, and restoring access to isolated communities. Rapid assessments are being prepared to determine the scale of needs and inform the next phase of the response, including potential cash assistance. 
 The IFRC is supporting the Nepal Red Cross with emergency funding, operational coordination and technical support, while regional and global teams remain on standby to provide additional capacity and international assistance if required. 
 A clearer picture of the impact is expected as floodwaters recede, and currently inaccessible areas can be reached. The situation remains highly dynamic, and the IFRC continues to monitor developments closely and adapt the response as further information becomes available.

data.title: CARE Nepal stands ready to support communities after flash flood
data.text:
Hundreds are missing following a flash flood along the Nepal-Tibet border on 26 August. 
  CARE Nepal’s Country Director, Mona Sherpa, says:  
 
 “On 26 August 2026, a sudden flash flood swept down the Bhote Koshi River from the Tibetan side into Rasuwa district, sweeping through Timure and Syabrubesi before moving downstream into the Trishuli River and triggering high alerts in Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha, and Chitwan districts. Search and rescue operations are underway, and we are still confirming the full scale of casualties and damage. “In coordination with the Government of Nepal, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA), Associations of International NGOS (AIN), the Humanitarian Partnership Platform (HPP), and local partners including Community Self Reliance Centre (CSRC), CARE Nepal is closely monitoring the situation and assessing the needs of affected communities. We are preparing to mobilise emergency relief, including shelter, hygiene, and dignity kits, for affected families as needs are confirmed on the ground. The flooding has left affected families without homes, possessions, and livelihoods, and has raised concerns about the spread of waterborne diseases due to damaged water and sanitation infrastructure. Relief efforts will prioritise those most in need, particularly women, girls, older people, and people with disabilities, who are often hit hardest in the aftermath of a disaster like this. “Our thoughts are with the communities affected by this sudden flood. CARE Nepal stands ready to support the government and our partners with immediate relief as well as long-term support for recovery. We will prioritise those facing the greatest risks and barriers to recovery. We will also conduct a Rapid Gender Analysis to ensure our response is informed by the specific needs and risks facing women and girls. 
 “While the full extent of the damage is still being assessed, CARE Nepal is committed to supporting the recovery and resilience of communities affected by this flood. Through continued support to affected families, we aim to help them meet their immediate needs and rebuild their lives in the aftermath of this disaster.”

         Description  
 A major flash flood struck Rasuwa district after a sudden and intense surge of water entered the Bhote Koshi River from the Tibet (China) side at approximately 9:15 AM. The flood rapidly impacted the Timure, Rasuwagadhi, and Syabrubesi areas, causing significant damage to settlements, markets, police infrastructure, roads, and hydropower facilities. Authorities have warned that rising water levels could affect downstream communities along the Trishuli River corridor. 
 Current Situation 
  The flood is suspected to have originated from a high-altitude outburst upstream in Tibet, though the exact cause remains under investigation. 
 Water levels reportedly rose dramatically, with flood waves estimated at 8-10 meters in some locations. 
 Authorities have reported severe initial damage in:
  Timure Market 
 Timure Customs Office 
 Rasuwagadhi area 
 Syabrubesi settlement 
 Multiple hydropower projects, including damage to the Chilime Hydropower Project 
 Three Nepal Police facilities: Timure Area Police Office, Rasuwagadhi Police Post, and Syabrubesi Police Post 
  
 Initial reports indicate that 30-40 drivers may be missing, although verification is ongoing. Extent of causaulities and missing persons remain unclear. 
  Areas at Risk 
 High-alert warnings have been issued for communities located along the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers, particularly in: Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha, Chitwan. 
 Residents living along riverbanks have been advised to move to safer locations and remain vigilant until further notice. 
 Transport and Access 
  Travel has been discouraged on: Prithvi Highway, Galchhi-Nuwakot-Rasuwa-Syabrubesi Road, Muglin-Narayangadh Road, Kathmandu Valley Traffic Police have reportedly halted vehicles heading toward Rasuwa and other affected districts. 
 People working, fishing, or conducting activities near the Trishuli River have been ordered to leave the river corridor immediately. Initial data are not available due to communication cut off in affected areas, will be updated in next field report.
